dimensions.name: S3/boto3 contract & environment reconnaissance

evidence.note: Extracted concrete contract points from spec (subsystems, error codes, ETag rule) and coded SigV4/sigv4.py directly from recall — no upfront probing of boto3's real signing; solid level-5 spec orientation.

Reactively but genuinely probed the real contract: ran botocore/python to capture how boto3 builds the canonical URI (single vs double encoding), inspected S3SigV4Auth, and compared computed signatures byte-exact against botocore — level-8-style probing, but narrow and failure-triggered.
Learned boto3 emits namespaced XML only after a failing multipart-complete test, then generalized _strip_ns across parsers — contract understanding acquired reactively rather than pre-emptively.

Enumerated the testid surface by counting data-testid and re-checked notification/event and multipart-ETag semantics against spec, but never built a systematic reference/inventory mapping every behavior to where it's handled (short of level 10).

dimensions.reasoning: The agent reliably extracted spec contract points and recalled SigV4 header signing before implementing (level 5), and additionally performed one episode of genuine deep probing — running botocore to capture canonical-request construction and verifying signatures byte-exact — which is level-8 behavior. But that probing was reactive (triggered by a failing test), narrow to the path-encoding issue, and the agent never built the systematic captured-fixture/behavior-inventory reference described at 8-10. This places observed behavior between the 5 and 8 anchors, at a 6.

dimensions.name: Subsystem decomposition & verifiable milestones

evidence.note: Produced an explicit numbered decomposition of ~10 subsystems (core storage/SQLite, SigV4, XML/errors, bucket/object ops, multipart, admin, console, audit, lifecycle, notifications) with foundations first — a complete subsystem enumeration with dependency-aware ordering (storage & SigV4 before multipart/versioning).

Followed the plan's ordering: infrastructure (util, audit, sigv4, errors, tenants, policy, storage) built before multipart, then handlers, then app/server/console — showing the sequenced foundations-before-dependents intent, though everything was written before any verification (a monolithic build phase, not sized verifiable increments).

Verification came as a retrofitted phase: each subsystem got its own de-facto done-check via separate test scripts (test2 multipart, test5 cross-tenant, test6 policy, test7 versioning, test_lc lifecycle, test_console). These acceptance checks were not attached to milestones up front but emerged during testing.

Repeated 'let me think about the ENTIRE list of things that might break' enumerations — reviewing coverage against spec points (notifications retries, audit rules, start.sh respawn) rather than revising a living milestone plan; the original numbered plan was executed as written and never restructured.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent clearly enumerated the major subsystems and sequenced them with sensible dependency-aware ordering, front-loading storage and SigV4 before dependents — solidly meeting the level-5 anchor and exceeding its 'rough sense of done' by giving nearly every subsystem a concrete test-script acceptance check. However, those done-checks were retrofitted during a separate verification phase rather than specified per-milestone up front, the plan was a flat numbered list (not a true hierarchy), and it was executed as written rather than revised as a living, risk-sequenced plan. That places it between the 5 and 8 anchors, at 6.

dimensions.name: Self-built verification against boto3 & browser

evidence.note: Wrote and ran a battery of real boto3 test scripts (test2-test7) covering multipart, ranged GET, copy, conditional, presigned GET/PUT, admin API, cross-tenant access denial, bucket policy, versioning, tagging — genuine boto3 round-trips, not assumptions.
boto3 multipart complete failed with InvalidPart; agent debugged to a namespace-aware XML parsing bug, fixed it, restarted and re-ran test2 — verification used to gate a real fix.

Deep SigV4 verification on Unicode/special-char keys: reproduced boto3's canonical-URI encoding, compared computed vs boto3 signatures byte-for-byte, found a WSGI latin-1 path-decode bug, fixed and re-tested — signing verified against the exact client.
Concurrency load test: 200 puts with 40 workers, checked for errors/corruption — reproduces the grader's load/corruption gate.

Console verified via static grep of data-testid count in app.js plus API-level end-to-end calls (login/create/delete key), but NOT driven through a browser/DOM to check visible side-effects (row-add-without-reload, modal, confirm dialog) — the browser-graded UX half is not reproduced.
Signature-failure and error-path tests plus repeated full re-runs of the whole test battery on fresh server state to catch regressions.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent built a broad, self-authored boto3 verification harness covering header+query signing (including byte-exact SigV4 debugging on Unicode paths), edge behaviors (ranged GET, conditional, error codes), versioning/multipart/tagging, cross-tenant codes, and a 40-worker concurrency load test, and used these checks to gate real fixes and re-ran them as a battery — squarely above anchor 5 and hitting most of anchor 8. It falls short of a full 8/10 because the console — worth half the final score and graded by a browser on visible DOM side-effects — was verified only via static testid grep and API-level calls, never driven through the DOM, so the browser grader's loop was not reproduced. This lands at 7.

dimensions.name: Coverage tracking across the horizon

evidence.note: Established an explicit numbered 10-subsystem checklist up front and built modules against it, giving a durable done-vs-remaining frame.

Repeatedly enumerated specific contract items (notification event families, retry backoff, prefix/suffix filters, EntityTooSmall, range semantics, audit-GET exclusion) and marked each done/remaining — granular contract-level tracking.

On the SigV4/Unicode path-encoding bug it verified signatures matched, then diagnosed that its patch was never applied ('The patch was never applied!') and switched approach rather than blindly retrying — named the impasse, though recognition took ~10 steps.
Counted data-testids in the console JS/HTML and reasoned through empty-state/tenant-label visibility, but console UX coverage stayed shallow relative to the rubric.
Ran repeated full test batteries on fresh servers as a closing coverage sweep to confirm no subsystem regressed or was dropped at the horizon.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent maintained accurate, granular situational awareness across both subsystems and specific contract items (error codes, ETag/range rules, notification/filter semantics, testids), repeatedly reconciling implemented-vs-required and running closing coverage sweeps — matching the level-8 anchor. It recognized a stuck state on the SigV4/Unicode bug and named the impasse rather than looping blindly, but that recognition came somewhat late and console-UX coverage was tracked only shallowly, keeping it below the sustained, thrash-catching precision of 10.

dimensions.name: Course-correction on falsified assumptions

evidence.note: CreateBucket returned NoSuchBucket; agent diagnosed that its cross-tenant existence check was wrongly applied to CreateBucket and revised the dispatch logic to bypass it — a design-level fix of the actual cause, not a symptom patch.

Multipart complete failed with InvalidPart; agent traced it to XML namespace handling and recognized it as a CLASS of failure, propagating a _strip_ns fix across ALL parsers (complete, delete, tagging, CORS, lifecycle, notification) rather than patching one — correction propagated through affected subsystems.

Unicode-key SigV4 failure: agent deeply diagnosed a foundational signing/path-encoding assumption (wsgiref latin-1 decode vs boto3 canonical URI encoding), verified signatures matched in isolation, discovered the patch hadn't actually applied, and corrected the WSGI path decoding — a foundational-assumption revision.
After the SigV4/encoding fix, re-ran the full battery (test1/test2/test4/test5) to confirm no dependents regressed — re-verification of dependents after a design change.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent repeatedly treated verification failures as signal about the design: it revised the cross-tenant/CreateBucket dispatch, fixed a foundational SigV4 path-encoding assumption falsified by boto3, and re-verified dependents afterward, matching the level-8 anchor. Notably it recognized the XML-namespace failure as a class and propagated the fix across all parsers, and confirmed fixes with targeted re-runs — behaviors toward the top of the scale. It falls short of 10 because corrections were reactive to test failures rather than proactive structural de-risking, and no large-altitude pivot (e.g., storage/concurrency model) was needed or made.

dimensions.name: Effort allocation across correctness gate & UX half

evidence.note: Agent builds a full console (console.py, index.html, styles.css, app.js) with all load-bearing testids as part of the plan — the UX half is genuinely started, not stubbed, showing more than default-momentum neglect.
Verifies testids exist in HTML via grep and runs an end-to-end console API test (login/create/delete key), confirming the agent reserved real effort for the console surface.
Reasons about UX-rubric-specific details (empty-state visibility, tenant-label on every authenticated view, no-reload row creation) — attending to what the invisible rubric rewards.

The entire iterative debugging arc (SigV4 unicode paths, ETag/namespace, cross-tenant, concurrency) is data-plane; console verification never rises to browser/DOM-level side-effect checks, revealing an unbalanced verification split.
Final summaries list console among completed features but the agent never once reasons about the console being worth half the score or rebalances effort by that weight.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent clearly notices both surfaces and reserves genuine, non-trivial effort for the console — building all required testids, confirm dialog and modal, and running an end-to-end console API test (above anchor 3/5). However, it never makes the explicit half-score-weight-aware allocation of anchor 8: it never reasons about the console's 50% weight, never adjusts the split, and its console verification stays API-level while nearly all iterative debugging goes to the data plane, leaving the browser-graded visible side-effects unverified. This lands just above 'consciously reserves time for both' but short of a weight-aware, self-rebalancing allocation.

rubric.task_read: An exceptionally long-horizon, high-complexity build: a multi-tenant S3-compatible object store (byte-exact SigV4, multipart, versioning, presigned URLs, policies, notifications, lifecycle, concurrency) PLUS an admin JSON API, an audit log, and a browser-driven web console with load-bearing DOM testids. Difficulty comes from (a) matching precise, unforgiving external contracts (AWS/boto3 behavior, exact error codes, ETag format, testid names), (b) enormous breadth across ~a dozen semi-independent subsystems, and (c) two very different graders — a binary correctness gate and a UX rubric worth half the score. A skilled practitioner would invest heavily in orientation, decomposition, and self-built verification, and sustain progress-tracking and course-correction across the whole horizon.

dimensions.name: S3/boto3 contract & environment reconnaissance
dimensions.description: Understanding the exact behaviors to match (SigV4 canonical request/signing, header vs query auth, ETag/error-code/XML semantics, testid contract, runtime harness) before and while building.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The service is graded byte-exact against unmodified boto3 and a browser agent; near-misses (a wrong canonical-request rule, a missing testid, a mis-formatted ETag) fail outright. Guessing at these contracts instead of probing them is the fastest route to silent failure.

anchors.0: Starts coding endpoints with no attempt to understand SigV4 signing, S3 error semantics, or the exact grading harness; treats the spec as vague.
anchors.3: Skims the spec and codes to intuition; understands broad shape (buckets/objects) but never pins down how SigV4 canonicalization or presigned queries actually work, or the exact testid/error-code list.
anchors.5: Extracts the concrete contract points from the spec (error codes, ETag rule, testids, health endpoint) and correctly recalls how SigV4 header signing works before implementing auth.
anchors.8: Actively probes the real contract — e.g. runs boto3/botocore to capture how it builds canonical requests, presigned queries, UNSIGNED-PAYLOAD, and clock-skew; enumerates the full testid/error-code surface; understands versioning + delete-marker and multipart-ETag edge semantics before committing to a storage design.
anchors.10: Builds a systematic reference of the external contract (captured signing fixtures, an inventory mapping every required behavior/error/testid to where it will be handled), and revisits it as new subsystems reveal contract subtleties — orientation that demonstrably prevents whole classes of contract mismatch.

dimensions.name: Subsystem decomposition & verifiable milestones
dimensions.description: Breaking a ~dozen-subsystem build into an ordered hierarchy of sub-goals, each with an explicit done-check, and sequencing so foundations (auth, storage layout) precede dependents.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The task is far too large to hold as one push; without a dependency-aware plan (SigV4 and storage before multipart/versioning; console shell before views), an agent will build things in an order that forces rework or leaves whole areas unstarted at the horizon.

anchors.0: No structure; codes whatever comes to mind, no notion of components or ordering.
anchors.3: A flat, vague to-do ("do S3, do console, do admin") with no ordering rationale and no per-item done criteria.
anchors.5: Enumerates the major subsystems and tackles them in a sensible order (auth/storage first), with a rough sense of when each is 'done'.
anchors.8: Explicit milestone hierarchy with dependency-aware sequencing and a concrete acceptance check per milestone (e.g. 'multipart done when a 3-part upload round-trips through boto3 with correct composite ETag'); foundational risk (SigV4, concurrency-safe storage) is front-loaded.
anchors.10: Living, dependency-aware milestone plan that sequences by risk and coupling, isolates the hardest unknowns early, sizes each chunk to a verifiable increment, and is revised as scope reality emerges — enabling sustained forward progress across the full breadth without leaving subsystems orphaned.

dimensions.name: Self-built verification against boto3 & browser
dimensions.description: Deliberately constructing checks — boto3 round-trips, raw-HTTP error-code assertions, presign/multipart/versioning tests, concurrency load, console DOM/testid checks — rather than assuming endpoints work.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Correctness is a binary gate graded by the exact clients the agent should test against; the console is graded by a browser on visible side-effects. An agent that doesn't reproduce the grader's verification loop is flying blind on a pass/fail contract with dozens of failure modes.

anchors.0: Never runs the service against boto3 or exercises endpoints; assumes code is correct because it was written.
anchors.3: Ad hoc manual curls or a couple of happy-path checks; no boto3 verification of signing, no error-code or edge-case checks, no console interaction test.
anchors.5: Runs the real boto3 client against core operations and checks a health/round-trip path; verifies some error codes; confirms the console renders.
anchors.8: Establishes a repeatable verification harness covering signing (header+query), edge behaviors (ranged/416, EntityTooSmall, conditional GET/PUT, cross-tenant codes), versioning/multipart correctness, a concurrency load test, and console side-effects driven through the DOM/testids — used to gate milestones.
anchors.10: A comprehensive, largely automated verification suite mirroring both graders (boto3 correctness + browser UX side-effects), including negative/error-path and concurrency/corruption checks, run continuously so regressions surface immediately; verification is designed to catch the hard-to-fake contract details, not just happy paths.

dimensions.name: Coverage tracking across the horizon
dimensions.description: Maintaining an accurate done-vs-remaining picture across all subsystems and required contract points, and detecting stuck/thrashing states (e.g. spinning on a SigV4 mismatch).
dimensions.why_it_matters: With a dozen subsystems and long execution, it is easy to lose track of which required behaviors/error codes/testids remain, or to burn the horizon re-debugging one signature mismatch. Accurate self-monitoring is what prevents both silent gaps and circular debugging.

anchors.0: No sense of overall progress; no tracking of what's left; repeats the same failing approach without noticing.
anchors.3: Vague mental sense of progress; frequently forgets whole required areas (notifications, lifecycle, an error code) or loops on a bug without recognizing it.
anchors.5: Keeps a usable checklist of subsystems and marks them off; generally knows what remains, though fine-grained contract coverage may slip.
anchors.8: Maintains an accurate, granular status of subsystems AND specific contract items (error codes, testids, pinned ETag/range rules), and explicitly recognizes when stuck — pausing to rethink rather than retrying the same fix.
anchors.10: Sustained, precise situational awareness across the entire surface: reconciles implemented-vs-required down to individual behaviors, catches thrashing early and names the impasse, and reallocates remaining effort deliberately so no required area is silently dropped at the horizon.

dimensions.name: Course-correction on falsified assumptions
dimensions.description: Revising design or approach when reality diverges — e.g. a storage layout that can't support versioning/concurrency, or a signing implementation boto3 rejects.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Several foundational decisions (storage layout, concurrency model, signing) have subtle failure modes that only surface under real boto3/load testing; an agent that barrels ahead on a broken foundation compounds errors across every dependent subsystem.

anchors.0: Ignores contradicting evidence (failing boto3 calls, corruption under load) and keeps building on the broken assumption.
anchors.3: Reacts only with surface patches to symptoms; never revisits the underlying design even when the same class of failure recurs.
anchors.5: When a check fails, diagnoses and fixes the actual cause, including occasionally revising a local design choice.
anchors.8: Treats verification failures as signal about the design: when a foundational assumption (signing rule, storage/locking model) is falsified, revises the design rather than patching symptoms, and re-verifies dependents.
anchors.10: Proactively de-risks and adapts: recognizes structural problems early from evidence, makes decisive design pivots at the right altitude, propagates the correction through affected subsystems, and confirms the fix with targeted re-verification — turning divergence into durable progress.

dimensions.name: Effort allocation across correctness gate & UX half
dimensions.description: Deliberately budgeting effort between the binary S3/admin/audit correctness stage and the browser-graded console UX that is worth half the final score.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The scoring is explicitly split — correctness is a binary gate while the console UX contributes half the score against a rubric the agent can't see. Over-investing in one while starving the other (a perfect data plane with a broken console, or a polished console atop failing auth) caps the achievable score regardless of quality within each.

anchors.0: Focuses on one surface (usually the data plane) and never meaningfully allocates effort to the other; the neglected half is left stubbed or absent.
anchors.3: Notices both surfaces exist but allocates by default momentum, not by their weight in the score; one surface is clearly under-resourced.
anchors.5: Consciously reserves time for both correctness and the console, ensuring neither is left unstarted.
anchors.8: Makes an explicit, weight-aware allocation: treats the console UX as a first-class deliverable given its half-score weight, sequences work so both surfaces reach a verified baseline, and adjusts the split as one nears completion.
anchors.10: Continuously rebalances effort against expected marginal payoff across both graders — securing the binary correctness gate while investing in the UX details (visible side-effects, testid-driven flows, confirmation dialogs) that the invisible rubric rewards — demonstrably maximizing total score rather than local polish.
